title: Actuators & Output
blurb: Turning signals back into motion and sound.

topics.name: Active Buzzer
topics.question: What is an active buzzer and how is it different from a passive one
topics.assetAlt: Exploded views comparing an active buzzer (housing, piezo bender, and PCB with built-in drive circuit) with a passive buzzer (housing, piezo disc, and plain PCB with pins, no internal oscillator).

sections.heading: Active vs passive
paragraphs: An active buzzer contains its own oscillator — apply DC and it sounds at a fixed pitch. A passive buzzer is a tiny speaker that needs a driving frequency. For simple alerts the active type is just digitalWrite HIGH/LOW.

sections.heading: Driving it
paragraphs: It is polarised, so orientation matters, and draws more than an LED — drive louder buzzers through a transistor rather than directly from a pin.

topics.hint: An active buzzer that stays silent on a HIGH pin usually has reversed polarity — and if you need melodies, you actually need a passive buzzer driven with tone().

topics.name: Servo Motor
topics.question: What is a servo motor and how do pulses set its angle
topics.assetAlt: Photo of a micro hobby servo with a translucent case, labelling the internal potentiometer, reduction gears, DC motor and electronic control circuit, with its three-wire connector in the foreground.
topics.summary: Angle from pulse width at ≈50 Hz.

sections.heading: Position from pulses
paragraphs: A hobby servo reads a ≈50 Hz pulse train and moves its horn to an angle set by the pulse width (≈1 ms → 0°, ≈2 ms → 180°). Internal feedback holds that angle against load.

sections.heading: Driving it
paragraphs: Use the Arduino `Servo` library, which generates the correct timing on a digital pin. Signal is logic-level; power should be separate.

topics.hint: A servo that twitches or browns out the board on movement is drawing current spikes the 5 V rail cannot supply — power it from an external 5–6 V source with a common ground.

topics.name: Stepper & Driver
topics.question: What is a stepper motor, and why does it always need a driver
topics.assetAlt: Wiring diagram of an Arduino Uno driving a 28BYJ-48 stepper motor through a ULN2003 driver board: four digital pins connect to IN1–IN4, and the driver board exposes separate 5–12 V motor-supply terminals.

sections.heading: Coils and drivers
paragraphs: Steppers move in fixed steps by energising coil pairs in sequence. Never drive them from a pin — a driver (ULN2003 for the 28BYJ-48, or A4988/DRV8825 for bipolar NEMA motors) sequences the coils and limits current.

sections.heading: Identifying wiring
paragraphs: Use a multimeter to find coil pairs (a pair shows continuity; across pairs is open) before connecting, so the step sequence energises the right windings.

topics.hint: A motor that vibrates in place but will not rotate has its coil wiring/sequence wrong — buzz out the coil pairs with a multimeter and re-map the driver outputs.

topics.name: Holding Torque
topics.question: What is holding torque, and why do steppers skip steps
topics.assetAlt: Graph of a typical NEMA 17 stepper motor torque-versus-speed curve: torque starts near 48 N·cm at standstill and falls steadily to under 10 N·cm as speed approaches 800 RPM.
topics.summary: The torque–speed limit of a stepper.

sections.heading: Discrete steps
paragraphs: A stepper moves in fixed angular increments and can hold a position by energising its coils — that static resisting force is holding torque, giving open-loop positioning without an encoder.

sections.heading: Torque vs speed
paragraphs: Available torque falls as step rate rises (the torque-speed curve). Push too fast or too hard and the rotor slips — it skips steps silently and loses position with no error reported.

topics.hint: A motor that stutters or silently loses position under load is past the torque-speed curve — slow the step rate and/or raise the driver's current limit to recover holding torque.
